summary.text: Legendre’s formula reduces the divisibility to prime-adic valuation inequalities, with a uniform floor inequality for \(a=4n+2\), \(b=2n+3\), and \(a+b=6n+5\) handling the underlying factorial ratio. The extra factors in \(108\) come from strict binary gains at moduli \(2\) and \(4\), checked by \(n\bmod 4\), and from the fact that the base-\(3\) digit sum of \(6n+5\) is at least \(3\).

full_proof.text:
Let
\[
K=4n+2,\qquad L=2n+3,\qquad M=K+L=6n+5.
\]
Then
\[
3K=12n+6,\qquad 3L=6n+9.
\]
Thus the assertion is precisely
\[
108\,K!\,L!\,(M!)^2\mid (3K)!\,(3L)!.
\]
We prove this by comparing the exponent of every prime on the two sides.

For a prime \(p\), write \(v_p(x)\) for the exponent of \(p\) in a positive integer \(x\). We shall repeatedly use Legendre's formula
\[
v_p(t!)=\sum_{i\ge 1}\left\lfloor\frac{t}{p^i}\right\rfloor.
\]
Only finitely many terms in this sum are nonzero. This formula follows by counting, for each \(i\ge1\), the multiples of \(p^i\) among \(1,2,\ldots,t\): every factor divisible by \(p^j\) is counted once for each \(i\le j\), and hence is counted exactly according to its exponent of \(p\).

We first establish the floor inequality that gives the basic factorial-ratio integrality. For all nonnegative integers \(a,b\) and every positive integer \(m\),
\[
\left\lfloor\frac a m\right\rfloor+
\left\lfloor\frac b m\right\rfloor+
2\left\lfloor\frac{a+b}{m}\right\rfloor
\le
\left\lfloor\frac{3a}{m}\right\rfloor+
\left\lfloor\frac{3b}{m}\right\rfloor. \tag{1}
\]
To prove this, write
\[
a=mA+r,\qquad b=mB+s,
\]
where \(0\le r,s<m\). Substitution into (1) cancels the common contribution \(3A+3B\), reducing the claim to
\[
2\left\lfloor\frac{r+s}{m}\right\rfloor
\le
\left\lfloor\frac{3r}{m}\right\rfloor+
\left\lfloor\frac{3s}{m}\right\rfloor. \tag{2}
\]
Because \(0\le r+s<2m\), the floor on the left is either zero or one. If it is zero, (2) is immediate. If it is one, then \(r+s\ge m\). Consequently
\[
\left\lfloor\frac{3(r+s)}m\right\rfloor\ge 3.
\]
The elementary inequality \(\lfloor x\rfloor+\lfloor y\rfloor\ge\lfloor x+y\rfloor-1\), applied to \(x=3r/m\) and \(y=3s/m\), gives
\[
\left\lfloor\frac{3r}{m}\right\rfloor+
\left\lfloor\frac{3s}{m}\right\rfloor
\ge
\left\lfloor\frac{3(r+s)}m\right\rfloor-1
\ge2.
\]
This proves (2), and therefore (1).

Apply (1) with \(a=K\), \(b=L\), and \(m=p^i\). Since \(K+L=M\), this yields, for every prime \(p\) and every \(i\ge1\),
\[
\left\lfloor\frac K{p^i}\right\rfloor+
\left\lfloor\frac L{p^i}\right\rfloor+
2\left\lfloor\frac M{p^i}\right\rfloor
\le
\left\lfloor\frac {3K}{p^i}\right\rfloor+
\left\lfloor\frac {3L}{p^i}\right\rfloor. \tag{3}
\]
Summing (3) over \(i\ge1\) and using Legendre's formula gives
\[
v_p(K!)+v_p(L!)+2v_p(M!)
\le v_p((3K)!)+v_p((3L)!). \tag{4}
\]
Thus the factorial ratio without the factor \(108\) is integral. We need the stronger assertion that the right side of (4) has enough additional powers of \(2\) and \(3\), because
\[
108=2^2 3^3.
\]
For primes other than \(2\) and \(3\), (4) already gives exactly what is needed. We now obtain the two extra powers of \(2\) and the three extra powers of \(3\).

First consider \(p=2\). For each \(i\ge1\), define the surplus at the \(i\)-th binary level by
\[
\Delta_i=
\left\lfloor\frac {3K}{2^i}\right\rfloor+
\left\lfloor\frac {3L}{2^i}\right\rfloor
-
\left(
\left\lfloor\frac K{2^i}\right\rfloor+
\left\lfloor\frac L{2^i}\right\rfloor+
2\left\lfloor\frac M{2^i}\right\rfloor
\right).
\]
Inequality (3) says that \(\Delta_i\ge0\) for every \(i\). We claim that in fact
\[
\Delta_1=1\qquad\text{and}\qquad \Delta_2=1. \tag{5}
\]
For \(i=1\), direct evaluation gives
\[
\begin{aligned}
\left\lfloor\frac K2\right\rfloor&=2n+1,&
\left\lfloor\frac L2\right\rfloor&=n+1,&
\left\lfloor\frac M2\right\rfloor&=3n+2,\\
\left\lfloor\frac{3K}2\right\rfloor&=6n+3,&
\left\lfloor\frac{3L}2\right\rfloor&=3n+4.
\end{aligned}
\]
Hence the expression in parentheses is
\[
(2n+1)+(n+1)+2(3n+2)=9n+6,
\]
whereas the sum on the numerator side is
\[
(6n+3)+(3n+4)=9n+7.
\]
Thus \(\Delta_1=1\).

For \(i=2\), we split according to the parity of \(n\). If \(n=2q\), then
\[
K=8q+2,\qquad L=4q+3,\qquad M=12q+5,
\]
and therefore
\[
\left\lfloor\frac K4\right\rfloor+
\left\lfloor\frac L4\right\rfloor+
2\left\lfloor\frac M4\right\rfloor
=2q+q+2(3q+1)=9q+2,
\]
while
\[
\left\lfloor\frac{3K}4\right\rfloor+
\left\lfloor\frac{3L}4\right\rfloor
=(6q+1)+(3q+2)=9q+3.
\]
Thus \(\Delta_2=1\) in this case. If \(n=2q+1\), then
\[
K=8q+6,\qquad L=4q+5,\qquad M=12q+11,
\]
so
\[
\left\lfloor\frac K4\right\rfloor+
\left\lfloor\frac L4\right\rfloor+
2\left\lfloor\frac M4\right\rfloor
=(2q+1)+(q+1)+2(3q+2)=9q+6,
\]
and
\[
\left\lfloor\frac{3K}4\right\rfloor+
\left\lfloor\frac{3L}4\right\rfloor
=(6q+4)+(3q+3)=9q+7.
\]
Again \(\Delta_2=1\), proving (5).

Summing all the binary-level surpluses, all of which are nonnegative and the first two of which contribute one each, gives
\[
2+v_2(K!)+v_2(L!)+2v_2(M!)
\le v_2((3K)!)+v_2((3L)!). \tag{6}
\]
This accounts for the factor \(2^2\) in \(108\).

Now consider \(p=3\). Legendre's formula gives a particularly useful identity. For every nonnegative integer \(t\),
\[
\begin{aligned}
v_3((3t)!)
&=\sum_{i\ge1}\left\lfloor\frac{3t}{3^i}\right\rfloor\\
&=t+\sum_{i\ge2}\left\lfloor\frac{t}{3^{i-1}}\right\rfloor\\
&=t+v_3(t!).
\end{aligned} \tag{7}
\]
Applying (7) to \(K\) and \(L\), and using \(K+L=M\), yields
\[
\begin{aligned}
v_3((3K)!)+v_3((3L)!)
&=v_3(K!)+K+v_3(L!)+L\\
&=v_3(K!)+v_3(L!)+M. \tag{8}
\end{aligned}
\]
It remains to show that \(M\) exceeds \(2v_3(M!)\) by at least three.

Let \(s_3(t)\) denote the sum of the digits in the base-three expansion of \(t\). The standard digit-sum form of Legendre's formula is
\[
2v_3(t!)=t-s_3(t). \tag{9}
\]
For completeness, if \(t=\sum_{j\ge0}d_j3^j\), where \(d_j\in\{0,1,2\}\), then
\[
\sum_{i\ge1}\left\lfloor\frac{t}{3^i}\right\rfloor
=
\sum_{j\ge1}d_j(1+3+\cdots+3^{j-1})
=
\frac12\sum_{j\ge1}d_j(3^j-1)
=
\frac{t-s_3(t)}2,
\]
which proves (9).

Here
\[
M=6n+5=3(2n+1)+2.
\]
Thus the least significant ternary digit of \(M\) is \(2\), and the remaining ternary digits are exactly those of \(2n+1\). Hence
\[
s_3(M)=2+s_3(2n+1).
\]
Since \(2n+1\) is positive, its ternary representation contains at least one nonzero digit, so \(s_3(2n+1)\ge1\). Therefore
\[
s_3(M)\ge3. \tag{10}
\]
Combining (9) and (10),
\[
M-2v_3(M!)=s_3(M)\ge3.
\]
Using this in (8) gives
\[
3+v_3(K!)+v_3(L!)+2v_3(M!)
\le v_3((3K)!)+v_3((3L)!). \tag{11}
\]
This accounts for the factor \(3^3\) in \(108\).

We can now finish prime by prime. The exponent of a prime \(p\) in the proposed denominator is
\[
v_p(108)+v_p(K!)+v_p(L!)+2v_p(M!).
\]
If \(p=2\), then \(v_2(108)=2\), and inequality (6) shows that this exponent is no greater than the exponent of \(2\) in \((3K)!(3L)!\). If \(p=3\), then \(v_3(108)=3\), and inequality (11) gives the same conclusion. If \(p\ne2,3\), then \(v_p(108)=0\), and the basic inequality (4) gives the conclusion.

Thus, for every prime \(p\), the exponent of \(p\) in
\[
108\,K!\,L!\,(M!)^2
\]
is at most its exponent in \((3K)!(3L)!\). By unique factorization, this is equivalent to divisibility. Consequently
\[
108(4n+2)!(2n+3)!((6n+5)!)^2
\mid
(12n+6)!(6n+9)!
\]
for every nonnegative integer \(n\). Therefore
\[
\frac{(12n+6)!(6n+9)!}
{108(4n+2)!(2n+3)!((6n+5)!)^2}
\]
is an integer for every \(n\ge0\), as claimed.
